name: Bhutanatha Temples, Badami
deity: Shiva as Bhutanatha, lord of beings
period: Early Chalukya, 7th–8th century, with later additions to the 12th century
dynasty: Badami Chalukya, with later Kalyani Chalukya additions
style: Early Chalukya Dravida, with a later Nagara group
summary: On the eastern shore of Agastya Lake in Badami, the Bhutanatha temples mirror themselves in still water, a Chalukyan Shiva shrine begun in the seventh century and finished by a later dynasty.

sections.history: On the east bank of Agastya Lake, below the red sandstone cliffs of Badami, stands the Bhutanatha group, the town’s great lakeside shrine to Shiva as Bhutanatha, lord of beings. The main temple belongs to the seventh and eighth centuries: the inner shrine and hall are the work of the Badami Chalukyas, while the outer hall facing the water was completed in the eleventh century under the Kalyani Chalukyas, so the building records a conversation across centuries. A second cluster, the North Bhutanatha or Mallikarjuna group on the opposite bank, is later still, of the eleventh and twelfth centuries, and in the northern style. Together they make one of the most picturesque corners of Chalukyan Badami.
sections.architecture: The main Bhutanatha temple is Dravida in form, its sanctum crowned by a three-tiered tower, with carved heads of kinnaras and gandharvas, the celestial musicians, along its walls. An inner hall leads to the shrine, and the later outer hall opens towards the lake, so the whole building seems to step down to the water. Stone ghats wrap the shore of Agastya Lake in flights of steps, and across the water the North Bhutanatha group rises in the northern style, its curving towers a contrast to the Dravida tower on the eastern bank.
sections.legends: Agastya Lake takes its name from the sage Agastya, and tradition links him with Badami, anciently called Vatapi, through the tale of the demon brothers Vatapi and Ilvala, who tricked sages into eating Vatapi in the guise of a meal. Agastya is said to have digested the demon and ended the trick for good. Local belief holds that the lake’s waters carry healing power, and the shrine of Bhutanatha, lord of spirits and beings, stands at its very edge, where pilgrims have long come to the shore.
sections.festivals: As in Shiva temples across Karnataka, Maha Shivaratri is the most important observance at Bhutanatha, and the lake edge is lively on festival days. Local fairs and the regional Chalukya heritage festivals of music and dance also draw people to the water. Confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Walk down to Agastya Lake at the quiet ends of the day and the Bhutanatha temples sit golden above their own reflection, the cliffs rising behind. Spend time with the carved faces of kinnaras and gandharvas on the walls, step through the hall to the sanctum, then follow the ghats round the water. The shore is also the town’s washing place and meeting place, so the scene is lived-in as well as ancient.

visit.timings: The lakeside temples are open to visitors during the day; the site is outdoors and the shrine keeps its own worship hours. Confirm timings and any ticket requirement locally.
visit.dressCode: Modest dress is appropriate, and footwear is left outside the shrine; steps and ghats can be slippery near the water.
visit.photography: Photography is generally welcome around the lake and the temple exterior; ask before photographing inside the shrine or worshippers.
visit.gettingThere: Badami is in Bagalkot district; the Bhutanatha temples stand on the eastern shore of Agastya Lake, a short walk or auto ride from the town centre. Badami has the nearest railway station, and the nearest airport is Hubballi.
